extracted.intended_audience: students in a proof-based undergraduate mathematics course (beginners to intermediate) writing proofs for homework and exams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for producing rigorous, convincing mathematical proofs for coursework and exams, including writing style, level of detail, problem-solving strategies, and standard proof techniques (case analysis, contradiction, induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must be convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a super convincing argument that your claim is true; if done correctly it should leave no doubt in a reader's mind (so long as this reader is familiar with the subject matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the argument into simple steps each of which can be properly justified. Justifications may be axioms, definitions, results proved in class, or earlier steps in the proof. The goal is to convince the reader familiar with the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break argument into simple justified steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the argument as a sequence of simple steps, each with an explicit justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each step should refer to a definition, axiom, previously proved theorem, or an earlier line in the proof. This decomposition is the core of making a proof convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly and in complete sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the proof like a short essay: clear, organized, using complete grammatically correct English sentences and equations where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equations when helpful, but write explanations in sentences. This helps the grader/readers follow the flow of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define variables and new terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure to define any new terms or variables that you are using.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by defining your variables and laying out the initial hypotheses (some trivial context can be omitted if obvious). Clear definitions prevent ambiguity later in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof structure: introduction, body, conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize proofs with an introduction (setup/definitions/hypotheses), the main argument, and a conclusion reminding the reader what was proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by stating what you will prove and the variables/assumptions; present the meat of the argument; end by restating the proven claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike a balance between being too vague (omitting necessary steps) and too tedious (including every trivial calculation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust detail based on audience: experts can accept terse references (e.g., 'by the Spectral Theorem'), novices need more steps, and computer-verifiable proofs require extreme detail. For coursework, give enough detail to convince the grader you understand the argument and could fill in omitted steps; when in doubt, add details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the problem and form intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reread the problem, identify hypotheses and goals, test simple examples, and develop intuition for why the claim might be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Getting a feel for the problem often suggests fruitful lines of attack and guides construction of a rigorous argument even if the intuition is informal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for equivalent or simpler formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for other ways of stating the problem that might be easier to handle (e.g., use equivalent criteria, contrapositives, or known theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrasing the statement can expose applicable theorems or simpler approaches (e.g., prove contrapositive if direct implication is hard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unroll and use definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall and apply the precise definitions relevant to the statement (e.g., what it means for a set to be a subspace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing that all necessary conditions from the definitions hold is often the direct route to a proof; 'unrolling' helps make hidden assumptions explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use given hypotheses effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully consider how each assumption in the problem might be used; revisit the problem statement if progress stalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some assumptions may look unnecessary but are intended to be used later; recognizing where to apply them is key to completing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work on special or simpler cases for insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve or analyze simpler versions (e.g., finite-dimensional, diagonal matrices) to gain insight into the general problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special cases often provide patterns or ideas that can be generalized, even though solving them does not by itself prove the full result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and revise your proof
rubrics_metrics.description: After finishing, reread the proof to ensure every claim is justified and the argument is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any step leaves you unsure, fill in more details. Verifying small steps and edge cases reduces the chance of errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis: cover all cases and inform the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When splitting a problem into cases, explicitly state which cases you consider and ensure they cover all possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the cases and give the argument for each separately, clearly indicating which case you are in. If cases are symmetric, you may use WLOG but justify that the other cases are identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Without Loss Of Generality' (WLOG) correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply WLOG only when other cases are identical up to relabeling or symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If cases are identical in structure, argue that solving one suffices; explicitly state WLOG and why it is valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction: state assumption and conclude contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement, assume its negation and derive a contradiction, then conclude the original statement must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a line such as 'Assume for sake of contradiction (negation of the statement)', proceed to derive the contradiction, point it out, and restate the proven claim. This method is useful for nonexistence results because the negation often gives extra usable hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by induction: follow standard outline and inform the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements indexed by integers, prove a base case, assume P(n), prove P(n+1), and conclude P(n) holds for all n ≥ base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell the reader what you are proving by induction and which variable you're inducting on, state and prove the base case m, assume P(n) (inductive hypothesis) and prove P(n+1) (inductive step), then restate the result. Make the structure explicit so the reader follows the inductive argument.
